name: fancy-memset (fm): SSE2 and AVX2 memset in x86-64 assembly
language: x86-64 assembly (GNU as) with a C benchmark harness
baseline: glibc memset (the harness's 'sys' row calls the system libc memset; glibc version not stated); the harness also times FreeBSD, Bionic and Solaris memset, a naive rep stos and a naive -O3 loop
workload: memset with fill value 0 over a range of sizes; bench.c does 16 warm-up calls, then 100000 calls at each of 64 buffer offsets, timed with rdtsc/rdtscp, warm cache.
claimed_speedup: AVX2 version: '10-370% faster than glibc memset', '300-400% faster than a naive loop compiled with -O3 by gcc/icc/clang', '50-470% faster than freebsd memset, for sizes larger than 64 bytes'. SSE2 version: '20-150% faster than freebsd memset', '5-100% faster than bionic memset'; no glibc figure for SSE2 ('don't know about glibc, idk how to force it to use sse2'). README says numbers 'are variable and depend heavily on sizes'.
compiler_and_flags: bench.c built with CFLAGS -O3 -g -fno-builtin (makefile); compiler name and version not stated; assembly files assembled with as or cc -x assembler-with-cpp; 'make erms=' builds the variant for CPUs without ERMS
hardware: CPU model not stated; x86-64 only (SSE2 or AVX2 versions); README discusses Intel CPUs with ERMS and AMD CPUs without ERMS
tradeoffs: x86-64 only. The AVX2 version needs AVX2 and the SSE2 version SSE2; selection is by which object you link (no runtime dispatch seen in the makefile). ERMS use is chosen at assembly time (makefile --defsym erms), so the build must match the CPU. Author notes that very small and constant-size memsets are better inlined by the compiler, so the benchmark does not cover them. No LICENSE file in the repo root, so the code cannot be assumed copyable.
caveats: Public benchmark code and flags, but no CPU model, compiler version or glibc version, so it falls short of tier A. The 'sys' row is whatever memset the test machine's libc resolved to. The glibc figure is given only for AVX2 and spans 10-370% with no per-size table committed to the repo; author could not force glibc onto its SSE2 path. Fill value is always 0 and the buffer is warm in cache, with 100000 repeated calls on the same region, which favours cache-resident behaviour. Last commit April 2022, no license.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch (extended) 'open source hand-optimized memcpy memset strlen memchr routines repository with benchmark table comparing against glibc or newlib or musl' returned a note on the HN thread 'A 100LOC C impl of memset, that is faster than glibc's' that mentioned fancy-memset by moon-chilled; repo, readme, bench.c and makefile then opened on github.com/raw.githubusercontent.com

name: mmemmove (AJ528): memmove in ARM Cortex-M assembly
language: ARM Thumb assembly (Cortex-M4 and M0+) with a C test harness
baseline: The toolchain's standard memmove() on an STM32WLxx build with arm-none-eabi-gcc (README calls it 'my standard memmove()' and does not name newlib, newlib-nano or a version)
workload: memmove calls profiled with the Cortex-M4 cycle counter on an STM32WLxx microcontroller; sizes, alignments and overlap cases behind the quoted range are not documented in the README.
claimed_speedup: 'In my testing, memmove_() is always faster than my standard memmove(). Sometimes it's only a few cycles faster, other times it is 7x faster.' Object size 'under 230 bytes' on arm-none-eabi-gcc.
compiler_and_flags: arm-none-eabi-gcc (version and optimization flags not stated)
hardware: STM32WLxx (Cortex-M4 core); README says the code is designed for Cortex-M4 and M0+ and probably works on other ARMv6-M and ARMv7-M cores
tradeoffs: Cortex-M (ARMv6-M, ARMv7-M) only. Exposed as a separate symbol memmove_() to be called explicitly, not a link-time replacement for memmove. GPL-3.0 copyleft is awkward for firmware. The same author's sibling mmemcpy README says that implementation is slower than the Cortex-M4 libc memcpy because it avoids unaligned accesses, so the M4 behaviour of mmemmove is not characterised.
caveats: First-party, unqualified range with no table of cycle counts, sizes or alignments. Baseline library is not named and the core on which the 7x figure was measured (M4 versus M0+) is not stated. No compiler flags. The repo includes a Greatest-based test comparing results with the standard memmove and a cycle-counter profile setup, but no published results. Very small project (0 stars).

name: fast-strlen.c (bjourne gist): multi-threaded memchr-based strlen
baseline: libc strlen (labelled 'strlen' in the gist's printed output; libc implementation and version not stated, glibc presumed on Linux)
workload: strlen of a single multi-gigabyte buffer of 'A' bytes (printed lengths 4000007776 and 1999999999), scanned 10 times per variant.
claimed_speedup: threaded_strlen 34.09 GB/s versus libc strlen 8.76 GB/s on Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz with gcc 9.4.0; 43.56 GB/s versus 16.84 GB/s on Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz with gcc 13.1.1 (about 3.9x and 2.6x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native fast-strlen.c -lpthread -o fast-strlen (gcc 9.4.0 and gcc 13.1.1); gist says to use gcc because clang optimizes away parts of the benchmark
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2650 v4 @ 2.20GHz; Intel Xeon W-2245 @ 3.90GHz
tradeoffs: Not a usable strlen replacement. The fast path deliberately triggers SIGSEGV to find the end of mapped memory, then fans memchr out over all online CPUs; the author says it 'heavily relies on undefined behavior' and exists to beat benchmarks. It only pays off for multi-gigabyte strings and occupies every core. No license.
caveats: Author wrote it for fun after a '{n} times faster' benchmark post. Tier A only in the narrow sense that code, flags and CPU models are public; the workload is artificial. In the same output the single-thread vectorised versions do not beat libc: strlen_avx2 7.86 versus libc 8.76 GB/s on the E5-2650 v4, strlen_avx2 15.36 and strlen_avx512 16.36 versus libc 16.84 GB/s on the W-2245. On the W-2245 the byte-by-byte slow_strlen also prints 16.87 GB/s, level with libc, which suggests memory-bandwidth limits and possibly a compiler builtin (inference, not confirmed). The first run header says 4.00GB, the second 2.00GB. Date is the gist's 'last active' date, not a commit date.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SWAR OR SIMD strlen strnlen strcpy faster than libc benchmark repository C header-only' returned the gist 'fast-strlen.c'; gist opened twice on gist.github.com
